reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a programming and DeFi bot demonstration on a locally forked blockchain, explicitly showing deployment, testing, price manipulation, and flash-loan arbitrage mechanics. The description promotes a paid course and discount, but the supplied material does not make a guaranteed-return claim or request viewers to transfer funds, surrender credentials, or join a deceptive scheme. The price manipulation is described as an artificial test condition rather than concealed as an ordinary investment result.

opening.argument: The video links a financial outcome directly to deploying and operating the bot. It instructs the viewer to start the bot, wait for an arbitrage opportunity, and then says the flash loan will be triggered "to obtain profit" and "in order to gain money." The workflow also requires replacing a value with an API key and deploying the flash-loan contract. This is not merely discussion of market theory: the title presents an arbitrage DeFi bot using flash loans, while the instructions connect configuration and activation to automated profit generation.

citations.quote: ARBITRAGE DEMONSTRATION DEFI BOT THAT USE FLASH LOANS
once there is an arbitration opportunity according to the configuration he will trigger the loan to obtain profit
Just replace here by your API Key.
now I'm going to deploy the contract used for FlashLow

rebuttal.rebuttal: The absence of an explicit guarantee does not remove the solicitation-like linkage. The material tells viewers how to configure and activate a bot, supplies an API-key step, and describes the resulting flash loan as a way to obtain profit. Calling the chain local also does not negate the fact that the demonstrated workflow is presented as a bot users can build and operate.

citations.quote: we have a fork of blockchain running locally in our machine
Just replace here by your API Key.
in order to gain money

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Those instructions show a technical demonstration, not a promise that viewers will earn money. The account and blockchain are part of a local test environment, and the stated purpose was to check whether the code worked. The quoted phrase about profit describes the bot's programmed objective, while the material does not establish that a viewer would obtain a reliable return or that funds must be transferred.

opening.argument: Several concrete risk signals appear together: crypto assets, a very large wallet, deliberate price manipulation, an artificial arbitrage opportunity, and a reported amount earned. The speaker says the account has a huge amount of Shiba Inu, proposes a very large purchase to create the opportunity, and then reports that "0.6" was earned. The description adds an external course link, a 40% discount, and urgency because the promotion is valid only for a limited time. Taken together, this presents a high-risk profit workflow alongside a commercial push, rather than a neutral explanation of ordinary trading.

citations.quote: huge amount of Shiba Inu
we will make a very large purchase that will generate an artificial opportunity
here we have the total we earned here. 0.6 it was not casual
Promotion valid for a limited time.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Describing the opportunity as artificial does not make the surrounding presentation low risk; it shows that the example depends on manipulating prices with a large crypto holding. The course link, discount coupon, and limited-time language add a commercial urgency signal. The demonstration's unusually controlled conditions therefore cannot reasonably be treated as evidence of normal, repeatable trading.

citations.quote: we will make a very large purchase that will generate an artificial opportunity
Know the syllabus at the link below:
Promotion valid for a limited time.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The risk signals are explicitly disclosed rather than concealed: the speaker calls the opportunity artificial and acknowledges that the strategy is not commonly repeatable and depends heavily on the market. The reported 0.6 is a test result, not a stated guaranteed return. A discount and course link show marketing, but they do not establish that viewers are being deceived about trading profits.

opening.argument: The educational framing functions as promotion for participation in a DeFi-bot course. The description tells viewers that they will learn to build bots to invest in DeFi, contrasts ordinary Uniswap use with using bots, and directs them to a marketplace syllabus. It then advertises a coupon and a limited-time discount. The video title and demonstration supply the technical proof-of-concept, while the surrounding message steers viewers toward buying instruction for a flash-loan arbitrage system. That commercial pathway matters because the promoted subject is a profit-oriented bot, not general programming education.

citations.quote: one of the bots you will learn to build in the course: use bots to invest in Defi.
Know the syllabus at the link below:
"Whales" do not invest in the market defi through sites like Uniswap.org, but through mevbots!
Use Defi_Brasil coupon to earn 40% off.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The course is not incidental context: viewers are told they will build investment bots, given a marketplace link, and offered a time-limited discount. The demonstration's claims about flash-loan arbitrage make the promotion materially financial. Calling this education does not change that its practical purpose is to move viewers toward acquiring and using a profit-oriented bot workflow.

citations.quote: one of the bots you will learn to build in the course: use bots to invest in Defi
Know the syllabus at the link below
Promotion valid for a limited time.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The description openly identifies the material as a course and explains its programming syllabus, so the commercial nature is not hidden. Educational marketing alone does not establish a scam. The supplied material also qualifies the trading example: it says repeatability is uncommon and market-dependent, and frames the class as checking whether the code works rather than guaranteeing purchaser returns.
